intro

A supermarket store order is a hundred-plus cases. The warehouse system already sends them heaviest first. What it never tells a new picker is where each case goes. Get layer one wrong, and eighty cases later, the pallet leans.
case1

This is Stack Right, a pallet trainer for Specs. You're on the pallet jack. Grab whatever's glowing, and a ghost shows exactly where it goes, at real size. The tag gives the layer, the count, and the weight. Drop it near the ghost, and it snaps square.
overhang
Hang it over the edge, and it slides back with the reason.
gap
Leave a gap, and it tells you that too.
layer1
Every mistake is counted, by rule. The next one lights up as soon as the last one lands, so there's only ever one thing to do.
layer2
Real freight isn't tidy. Sacks, cartons, trays of tins, and the odd long one.
layer3mixed

Layer three mixes sizes. The big water cases go first, and the juice fills the strip they leave. It's turned ninety degrees, so the joints cross the layer below. None of it is hand-placed. The plan is computed from the case sizes.
hill
Real layers don't always come out even. There's only enough soup for half a layer, so it goes at the back and leaves a step. The trays of tins fill the front, two high, and it's level again.
built

I pick orders in a warehouse, so I built this from my own shifts. Clad's plan-lens skill turned my answers into a design brief. I corrected its premise, because real orders already come heaviest first. Then Clad built the lens through the Lens Studio M C P, tested by a self-test driver and seven Leaf scenarios.
complete
Thirty-four items, five layers, a hundred and forty centimetres, under the height line. Time, and mistakes by rule.
close
Real orders are three times this size. Stack Right lets a new picker build them right, before they touch real stock. It's built and tested in the Lens Studio preview. Next is a real pair of Specs.
